articles.title: Harley-Davidson spins out LiveWire as its own electric motorcycle brand
articles.summary: Harley-Davidson is spinning out its electric motorcycle division as a standalone company called LiveWire. A new electrified model will be unveiled in July.
articles.body: LiveWire, the first electric motorcycle from Harley-Davidson, will now become its own standalone brand. The Milwaukee-based company announced that it would be spinning out its electric motorcycle division as its own company with a distinct lineup and a tailored retail experience. Harley-Davidson plans to unveil the “first LiveWire branded motorcycle” on July 8th to coincide with the International Motorcycle Show. It’s a similar move to how Harley-Davidson approached its new electric bicycle company, Serial 1. The idea is that LiveWire continues to benefit from its relationship with its parent company while also forging its own brand identity that is distinct from Harley-Davidson. It’s a shift from how the company approached its current LiveWire model, in which the Harley-Davidson logo is front and center, while the LiveWire brand is practically nonexistent. And it’s a sign that going forward, Harley-Davidson is interested in letting its electrified models stand on their own terms. “With the mission to be the most desirable electric motorcycle brand in the world, LiveWire will pioneer the future of motorcycling, for the pursuit of urban adventure and beyond,” Jochen Zeitz, chairman, president, and CEO of Harley-Davidson, said in a statement. “LiveWire also plans to innovate and develop technology that will be applicable to Harley-Davidson electric motorcycles in the future.” [Image: There’s a new logo and a new “virtual” headquarters, with engineering teams stationed in Silicon Valley and Milwaukee. LiveWire will work with Harley-Davidson dealerships as an independent brand, with a blend of digital and physical retail formats. Asked whether this will include online ordering, a Harley-Davidson spokesperson responded with a cautiously worded statement. “It depends on the state in which you live,” the spokesperson said. “LiveWire is creating a purchase path that allows us to meet the expectations for a digital-first purchase experience, supported by a network of committed dealers that allow customers to choose their path and engagement model.” The question is whether this branding strategy will lead to better sales for Harley-Davidson’s electric models. Last year, Reuters reported that the company’s plan to appeal to a younger generation of motorcyclists with the LiveWire was struggling, with most of the preorders coming from older or preexisting customers. Harley-Davidson’s overall sales have been stagnant lately after hitting a low point in 2018. The problem could be that the price, which starts at $29,799, isn’t that much cheaper than a Tesla Model 3. Dealers told Reuters that many younger customers were turned off by the price tag. Harley-Davidson is also facing some stiff competition from rivals like Zero Motorcycles, which recently teamed up with power sports manufacturer Polaris on a new lineup of electric-powered ATVs and snowmobiles. And as the broader world of transportation shifts to electric, the company will be under increasing pressure from its shareholders to prove its vision for the future can be profitable.

articles.title: Amazon’s AI shopping assistant can now edit your grocery lists and gift registries
articles.summary: Amazon is updating its Alexa for Shopping assistant with several new features, including the ability to manage grocery lists and gift registries, as well as answer billing questions.
articles.body: Amazon is adding several new features to its AI shopping assistant, including ways to create, edit, and move items between shopping lists and gift registries. As an example, Amazon says you can now ask Alexa for Shopping to “Create a new shopping list” or “Show me what’s left on my wedding registry.” The ecommerce giant has continued to expand on its Alexa for Shopping assistant since its official launch in May, while resisting third-party AI shopping agents from companies like Meta and Perplexity. Alexa for Shopping lives next to the search bar across Amazon’s app and website, and can do things like set price alerts, compare items, and automatically purchase products when they drop below a set price. Along with the ability to manage registries and lists, Alexa for Shopping can now update your delivery instructions, answer billing questions about unrecognized charges and refunds, as well as pause and change recurring deliveries. These features are rolling out to customers in the US.

articles.title: In 1964, Georgian-style house was built in Charlotte, North Carolina; Decades later, Brooklyn Decker and Andy Roddick transformed the 7,000-square-foot fixer-upper into a colourful family home blending historic charm with personal design touches
articles.summary: Brooklyn Decker has opened the doors to the North Carolina house she and her husband, former tennis champion Andy Roddick, have spent years turning into a
articles.body: Brooklyn Decker has opened the doors to the North Carolina house she and her husband, former tennis champion Andy Roddick, have spent years turning into a true family home. The 7,000-square-foot Georgian-style house in Charlotte dates to 1964 and arrived in their lives as a genuine fixer-upper. One room had already caved in and water poured through the ceiling when they first saw it. Most of the house had barely been touched since it was built. Still, Decker, who grew up in the state, saw something worth saving: a solid neighbourhood, good bones, and the chance to put down roots after years of moving. What followed was a full gut renovation that kept the home’s traditional character while filling it with the colour and energy of family life.Brooklyn Decker’s house that needed everythingWhen the couple first walked through the property, they knew the work would be serious. Beyond the collapsed ceiling and water damage, the interiors felt frozen in time. Decker and Roddick became only the second owners. They had renovated homes before, but nothing on this scale. “We’d moved so many times [before this house],” Decker told Architectural Digest. “And we were excited to try something new. For us, that meant a historic house with some old Southern bones.” They brought in Ruard Veltman Architecture to rethink the structure and Stanwick Dunham for the contracting. The goal was to respect the original Georgian lines while making the house work for everyday family life.Brooklyn Decker’s design that stayed personalDecker took charge of the interiors herself. Over the past six years she has turned her love of decorating into professional work, including as a design partner with the firm By Idiots. She wanted to keep the house’s early character; what she described as “old English meets early Georgian meets Shaker”, while introducing modern comfort. Wallpaper with natural scenes, vintage patterned rugs, and a soft palette of muted greens, reds, blues, and yellows began to appear. The result was layered rather and a mix of history and the present.Colour led by Brooklyn Decker’s kidsThe biggest shift in the design came from listening to their children. Decker’s son Hank, now 10, and Stevie, 8, were given real say in the rooms around them. “When our kids became older, we really wanted to incorporate and take seriously what they wanted,” Decker explained. “Because, how cool to be eight and actually have some say in the space around you? So now the house is a hodgepodge of explosive colour, a lot of which is totally inspired and dictated by them.” The once-formal spaces now carry bright, playful energy that still sits comfortably inside the traditional architecture.A home that feels lived inThe finished house balances elegance with the mess and joy of family life. Original features remain visible, yet every room feels ready for daily use. Decker has described the process as both challenging and rewarding, a project that finally let the family settle into a place with history and heart. For a couple that had moved often, the Charlotte house represents a decision to stay put and build something lasting, one colourful room at a time.More on Brooklyn DeckerBrooklyn Decker is an American model, actress, and interior designer who rose to fame as a Sports Illustrated Swimsuit cover star before transitioning into film and television roles. She has appeared in movies like ‘Just Go with It’ and the series ‘Grace and Frankie’. Married to former tennis champion Andy Roddick, she shares two children with him and has increasingly focused on design work. A Southern girl at heart, she is known for her down-to-earth style and lends a warm, personal element to her professional projects and family life.DISCLAIMER: Figures presented in this article are derived from various public sources and are considered approximate unless explicitly noted. articles.title: Saath Nibhana Saathiya fame Devoleena Bhattacharjee defends women’s choice of keeping Karwa Chauth
articles.summary: Television actress Devoleena Bhattacharjee, who became a household name after playing the role of Gopi Bahu in Saath Nibhana Saathiya, celebrates all the
articles.body: Television actress Devoleena Bhattacharjee, who became a household name after playing the role of Gopi Bahu in Saath Nibhana Saathiya, celebrates all the festivals with the same excitement. Recently, the actress shared her opinion on Karwa Chauth, and the people celebrating the occasion.Devoleena, who is known for expressing her opinions freely and is quite vocal about her thoughts, took to her X account to speak about the festival of Karwa Chauth.On Thursday, the actress took to her X, formerly Twitter, and shared a long note in which she shared her perspective on the festival.She wrote, “Happy Karwa Chauth to all the beautiful ladies celebrating today. I’ve never kept a Karwa Chauth fast because, in Bengali and Assamese cultures, it isn’t a tradition. We may not have every ritual, but we celebrate so many festivals with all our hearts. So why not Karwa Chauth? Honestly, I do feel like keeping it someday. But I’m scared I won’t be able to manage a whole day without water. I fast every Monday and sometimes on Ekadashi, but water fasting? That’s a different story! But that’s not even the point. I genuinely feel that for many couples, this is a love language. I’ve seen women celebrate it happily, and today, so many husbands fast alongside their wives. So why bring feminism, patriarchy and judgment into someone else’s celebration? You don’t believe in it? Don’t celebrate it”.She went on to add that nobody is judging them but it’s not right to spoil someone else’s happiness.She further shared, “Mothers fast for their children, for their families. So if someone wishes to fast for her husband one day, why should that be a problem? As long as it’s a personal choice and nobody is forced into it, let people celebrate love the way they want to. And a little personal note, Shaan comes from a Muslim family, yet every Karwa Chauth, he asks me, ‘Tum rakhogi kya fast?’. And every year, I say, with a heavy heart, ‘Dekhte hain, next year’. I’m still breastfeeding, so hopefully next year! Because honestly, husbands deserve to feel special and loved too, don’t they? We do intermittent fasting, try keto and follow all kinds of diets for ourselves”.She concluded the note saying, "But when it comes to fasting for a husband, suddenly everything becomes about patriarchy and feminism? Ladies, thoda chill karo! Love is personal. Traditions are personal. Celebrations are personal. Let people choose what makes them happy. Happy Karwa Chauth to everyone celebrating! May your love always grow stronger."Devoleena got married to Shanawaz Shaikh on 14th of December 2022 in a private ceremony. Only close friends and family attended the wedding ceremony. The couple welcomed their first child, a baby boy named Joy in December 2024.Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Rivian’s R2 is officially its best-selling vehicle
articles.summary: Rivian reports $2.15B in Q3 revenue as the R2 becomes its best-selling EV, supported by surging software revenue and licensing deals with Volkswagen.
articles.body: Rivian reported its third quarter earnings of 2026, providing us a closer look at the company’s financial health as it ramps up production of its all-important R2 electric vehicle — which is now, for the first time, outselling all of Rivian’s other EVs. Rivian said it brought in $2.155 billion in revenue, a 38 percent increase compared to the $1.558 billion in Q3 2025. Of that amount, $1.55 billion came from automotive revenue, which is up 36 percent year over year. Comparatively, the company reported $605 million from software and subscription services, a 45 percent increase year over year. As EV sales slow down, the company is seeking to make more money from its digital products, including the Autonomy Plus package. Automotive gross profits were on an upward trajectory, a sign that the company’s finances were improving as it delivered more vehicles. Rivian made $176 million in gross profit this quarter, a $152 million improvement compared to the same time last year. The company still lost $80 million in Q3 automotive gross profits, which is much better than the $130 million loss a year ago. In other words, Rivian is losing less than it did a year ago because they sold more cars and made more money per vehicle. (Also, the company continued to sell pollution credits to other carmakers, and also received a tariff refund from the government — all of which was recorded as revenue.) Rivian brought in $256 million in profit in software and services, up $102 million from last year, with a strong 42 percent profit margin. Most of this cash came from licensing their tech to Volkswagen, alongside customer subscriptions for Rivian’s Autonomy Plus driving features. In many ways, Rivian’s tech partnership with Volkswagen and software sales are currently paying the bills, keeping the company profitable overall while it absorbs a lot of heavy upfront costs from launching the R2. Earlier this month, Rivian reported a record sales quarter, with 19,751 vehicles produced and 19,248 delivered. That represents an 85 percent year-over-year increase in production and a 45 percent jump in deliveries. (For a direct-to-consumer automaker like Rivian, deliveries serve as a proxy for sales.) Rivian doesn’t break down sales by model, so we don’t exactly how many R2s have reached customers so far. But the company said that the R2 is now the “best-selling Rivian vehicle by volume,” outselling the R1T and R1S, as well as the Electric Delivery Van (EDV). “We had great results with R2 becoming our best selling vehicle by volume in the third quarter,” Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe said in a statement, ahead of the company’s earnings call this afternoon. “Customer and media feedback on R2 has been exceptional.” The R2 was designed from the ground up to be Rivian’s higher-volume, mass-market offering — and by overtaking the company’s more expensive, lower-volume legacy vehicles, it seems to be doing just that. Still, the R2 isn’t bringing in the bulk of the revenue yet, as indicated by Rivian’s use of the phrase “by volume.” Most of the money is still coming from the VW partnership and its software division. But that could change once Rivian starts shipping the more affordable versions of the R2, like the $55,485 Premium trim (coming in late 2026), the $49,985 Standard Long-Range (early 2027), and the $46,495 Standard (late 2027). Developing…

articles.title: Reddit will force everyone to log in
articles.summary: Reddit is becoming a ‘logged-in-only experience,’ says CEO Steve Huffman.
articles.body: Reddit is announcing a huge shift: It’s going to start requiring users to log in. Right now, you can browse Reddit without having an account, and the site is generally a great resource for crowdsourced information on a whole range of topics. I know I’m not the only person who appends “reddit” to a lot of Google searches to find answers to things written by actual humans instead of robots. But that openness has made it a target for scraping and automated traffic, leading Reddit to file lawsuits over alleged unauthorized access of its data and make product changes like limiting access to “Old Reddit.” There’s no definitive timeline on when this change will roll out to all users, or how the site will work if you’re logged out. (If I send my friend a link to a thread and they aren’t logged in, what will they see?) To start, Reddit will test the logged-in requirement in “select markets outside the US” in the “coming months,” according to CEO Steve Huffman. “We’ll look at the impact on the user experience, on our business, and on the whole Reddit ecosystem, figure out where the right boundaries are, and go from there.” Reddit has also rebuilt and is rereleasing the Reddit app’s incognito mode. Huffman claims the login requirement is better for Reddit’s user experience and its ads business and is “more protective of Reddit data.” The “vast majority” of unauthorized Reddit access happens “through our logged-out experiences,” though the company will still strike licensing deals of its data with companies, like the deals it made with OpenAI and Google in 2024. Huffman notes that Reddit does not need to know a logged-in user’s identity — “Honestly, we don’t want to know” — just that the user is logged in at all. And he says that more logged-in users lets the company deliver “more relevant ads.” “This is a big change for Reddit, where we’ve allowed logged-out access to basically all of Reddit for the last two decades,” Huffman says. “And I don’t know about you, but as someone whose life has been defined by the open internet, it’s a big change for me. But I’ve come to the conclusion that this is the right decision for our platform and the right decision for our business.” Reddit is making this announcement alongside its Q3 2026 earnings, which were released today. Search traffic was “down meaningfully” in Q3, Huffman says in the company’s shareholder letter, with logged-out traffic and web traffic being the most heavily impacted. “During October, we have seen that search traffic has dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week,” Huffman says. However, Huffman notes that app and logged-in daily active unique users make up “over 80% of the monetization on Reddit,” which he says “speaks to the strength of Reddit as a destination and the impact of our ongoing product work.”

articles.title: Reddit’s CEO says Google’s AI Mode ‘does not drive traffic’
articles.summary: Reddit CEO Steve Huffman said in an earnings call today that Google’s AI-powered search modes do not help with traffic to the platform.
articles.body: Reddit CEO Steve Huffman said in an earnings call today that Google’s AI-powered search modes do not help with traffic to the platform, echoing problems facing other websites and publishers. As part of its Q3 2026 earnings, Reddit revealed that search traffic in October has “dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week,” and he attributes part of the company’s struggles with Google traffic to how AI Mode and AI Overviews change the search experience. “The reality is, AI Mode does not drive traffic,” Huffman says. “Not for us, and not to anybody, as far as I know. That’s just a fundamental shift in how Google works. It used to be a traffic driver, now it’s not.” He says that AI Overviews and AI Mode have “evolved a lot” and now, at a “minimum,” push “everyone down the search page.” Huffman also says that Reddit believes its content that’s machine-translated into other languages is being ranked lower in search results, which he says would primarily affect the company outside the US. However, Reddit is still a “top search term in Google,” Huffman says. “This doesn’t say anything about the internet consumers’ demand for Reddit. People still want Reddit. It says Google is not sending them to Reddit the way they used to.” He also says that Google is “crawling us as hard as ever, so the demand hasn’t changed from their point of view, either.” (Google’s business has been affected by AI Mode, too: it said yesterday that it’s seeing “lower monetization” in AI Mode ads, though it’s now bringing AI ads to more countries.) To try and combat the search referral difficulties, Reddit is working to make the platform a “direct, sticky, daily destination.” Yesterday, it introduced a “For You” feed with recommendations related to your interests, and in August, it started testing an experiment that uses AI to turn posts into short videos. Reddit also announced today that it’s going to force everyone to log in, which Huffman claims will be “better for user experience, better for our ads business, is more in line with safety regulations, and more protective of Reddit data.”

articles.title: The touchscreen MacBook Pro is just a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen
articles.summary: Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is thinner, lighter, and has an incredible OLED display. But the touchscreen feels like an afterthought.
articles.body: Apple’s long-awaited touchscreen MacBook Pro is finally here. I got to try this MacBook that, according to the last two Apple CEOs, shouldn’t exist. The most surprising thing is how normal it is. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display (what a name) has one of the nicest screens I’ve seen on a laptop. The current Mini LED MacBook Pros are great, but the OLED has those even inkier blacks. It also gets super bright, with incredibly rich colors and infinite contrast. Apple calls it a “reference-caliber display,” which is a very Apple-y marketing term, but it walks the walk by being the first laptop display with support for Apple CMF 2026 color modes. [Media: But Apple didn’t spend 16 years saying it wouldn’t put an OLED in a laptop. The hallmark feature — the thing Apple was never going to do until it did — was the touchscreen. How would Apple prove that touchscreens on laptops aren’t “ergonomically terrible”? What magic would it bring to this input method that makes us go, “Ah-ha! Apple took its time, but it really figured it out”? And it’s just a touchscreen. [Image: We’re just normal touchscreen laptops. Just innocent touchscreen laptops. Of course, I’m glad Apple is finally doing this. There’s no harm in accommodating people’s natural urge to reach out and touch something on a screen. But there’s also no magic. You can poke and swipe at the screen. Hooray! Some UI elements in macOS 27 Golden Gate and certain apps either magnify or expand a little when you tap them. It’s cool and all, but it doesn’t exactly look like it’ll reinvent how we use laptops. (Better luck in future macOS updates, I guess?) Over a decade ago, touchscreen laptops were supposed to be revolutionary. Microsoft gave Windows 8 a whole new touch-optimized UI. Laptops started flipping and folding and getting all weird and fun. Then, Windows 8 crashed and burned, and convertible laptops became just another product segment as opposed to redefining how a laptop looks and works. Apple waited it all out, realized no one cared that much, added a touchscreen with some minor UI improvements, and went, “Okay, enjoy macOS with some swiping.” [Image: This demo from a pro photographer used bracketed exposures and a vibe coded app to composite the images into one interactive photo. The taps and swipes on the screen were a natural way to collage the imagery, but a mouse or trackpad works too. It’s kind of boring, but maybe a winning move. It finally rips off the Band-Aid for Apple and sets the table for touchscreens to one day come to much more attainable laptops, like the MacBook Air and Neo. Apple still has lots of touch-based devices for people who want to prioritize that. But this is just normal now: You have a laptop with a keyboard, trackpad, and a touchable screen for whenever you want to poke at it. It’s all very strategic, as is usually the case with Apple. But it’s hard not to wonder that it could have done more. Looking at the touchscreen settings menu, I saw that most touch gestures just map to things you can already do on the trackpad. At Apple’s event, I sat in on briefings that included professionals who recently started using the touchscreen MacBook Pro. Touching the screen wasn’t redefining their workflows or how they practice their craft — they still defaulted to keyboard and trackpad functions. The touchscreen was just a bonus. When I asked a few of them if they wished the MacBook Pro included Apple Pencil support, nearly all of them said sure, that’d be cool, too. Because the more options, the better. Apple took over a decade to come around to the touchscreen. Don’t hold your breath for Pencil support or a 360-degree hinge. [Image: This is fine. The new OLED and lighter chassis are just as important as the touchscreen in making the new MacBook Pro feel special. The Dynamic Island is a nice upgrade over the notch. And bringing back the illuminated Apple logo is just fun! It’s actually what got the biggest reaction from the crowd during John Ternus’ incredibly brief presentation. This new MacBook Pro looks great as a whole, but there’s more magic in that lid logo than the touchscreen. Before the event, I wondered how Apple could make a touchscreen laptop better. And, well, it just made a touchscreen laptop. Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

articles.title: The Apple Pencil turned the Duo into my new favorite notebook
articles.summary: The iPhone Duo’s Apple Pencil compatibility means it can do a pretty good impression of a notebook.
articles.body: Apple’s $2,000 folding phone is a surprisingly good stand-in for a $20 notebook. Believe me; nothing gets me going quite like a new notebook. This one will be different, I think. This time, I really will take it everywhere. Inspiration can strike at any moment, and you have to be ready, says David Sedaris in that one MasterClass I watched on a flight. With this one special new notebook, I will see the world differently. I’ll steal moments for myself to write, rather than pulling out my phone to scroll at every opportunity like a trained monkey. And a few weeks, a month, or maybe a year later, I’ll concede that it didn’t change everything and add it to my notebook graveyard. At least they all look nice on the corner of my desk? The iPhone Duo is not a notebook — although it is the first iPhone to support the Apple Pencil. Even so, I can see the new notebook effect in the eyes of the people I talk to about the Duo. “Is that the new iPhone?” the conversation starts. I hand over the phone and give them the short version of our 26-minute review: It’s nice, it’s kind of heavy and chunky, you should wait for the second generation. They nod, but I can tell they still want one anyway. They’re tired of their big/aging/boring phone, they tell me. And this one would be different. It’s hard to argue against. It really is a different phone. Its new form factor lets you actually use it in meaningfully different ways. The Duo can act like a vintage Hasselblad with a waist-level viewfinder. It can be a book-shaped e-reader. And with this week’s iOS 27.2 update officially adding that Apple Pencil support, it can also be a notebook. That’s the USB-C Apple Pencil, to be specific, so there’s no pressure sensitivity. You do still get the ability to “scribble” handwriting that’s automatically turned into text in apps like Messages or Safari, as you can on the iPad. But even with the basic stylus, there’s a lot of fun to be had doodling and writing notes out by hand. I asked for some Pencil-friendly app suggestions and downloaded a handful. I used the native Notes app to scribble down some article ideas. I set my five-year-old loose on a blank note, to his delight (the phone survived the encounter, too). But having the stylus in my hand led me on an unexpected side quest: turning the whole phone into a notebook. Why not? It’s notebook-shaped. Notebooks are nice and help you express creativity. Phones are bad attention-stealing machines, or something. Maybe I could cajole the Duo into being something less distracting, more input-friendly. I put together a minimalist home and lockscreen designed around this theory. I won’t lie, it’s pretty nice. But I don’t think I curated my way out of the new-notebook trap, even if it was a fun exercise. There aren’t many apps ready to take advantage of the new stylus support. Notes, unsurprisingly, is where the Pencil is at its best. When you use the Pencil for handwriting in the app, you can enable the auto-refine handwriting feature that neatens up your writing while still keeping its unique characteristics intact. This has been available on the iPad since 2024, and it’s particularly useful on the Duo’s comparatively small screens. It occasionally gets tripped up by some of my scrawl that it either doesn’t know what to do with or misinterprets — it kept insisting on turning a “u” into an “o” in one instance. And it works after a small delay when you pause your writing, which I can see being distracting if I really want to get into a flow state. But it’s a nice middle ground between my untidy scribbles and full handwriting-to-text conversion and very handy for something like a grocery list. The Notes app also has a big homescreen widget that kind of turned the phone into a notebook, but wasn’t nice to look at. After some more digging, I found almost exactly what I’d been looking for: TypeDraw. [Image: Writing on the Duo’s inner screen is pretty delightful. It’s a $4.99 one-time purchase, and it’s optimized for the Duo. When you launch the app, it turns the cover screen into the front of your notebook. To flip to a page, you can either swipe on the cover screen or open the whole phone. It’s a delight. TypeDraw isn’t really for power note-takers the way other apps like Bear are. You can’t add tags or links between notes, and you’re limited to one notebook. But it automatically creates a table of contents at the beginning based on the headings of your notes, so you can skip right to the section you’re looking for. Plus, if you drag your finger along the “elastic” on the cover, it’ll stretch and snap back, complete with satisfying haptics. I have zero regrets about the five bucks I spent on this app. Using the Apple Pencil with the Duo gave me one more reason to love the matte finish on the inner screen. There’s just a bit of resistance moving the pencil across the display that feels more satisfying than the lifeless plastic-on-glass effect of writing on the cover screen. It’s not going to feel like using a Remarkable tablet or anything, but it’s nice. The Pencil has one other neat trick — it can stick to the Duo’s hinge magnetically when the phone is closed. The pencil is longer than the phone, so it’s an awkward fit, but it’s been a handy way to carry both around the house as I relocate throughout the day. I was only, like, 60 percent serious when I set out to turn the Duo into a notebook, but I actually liked the idea the more I got into it. Reimagining my homescreen around creating rather than consuming feels like a worthwhile cause, and I’m planning to live with it for a while to see if it inspires any changes in my phone habits. To that end, I also set up a shortcut to launch TypeDraw whenever I open the inner screen. [Image: This is my new new minimalist homescreen. But I think the most useful part of this exercise was examining, once again, how much stuff I really need on my homescreen. I can get most things done with a Spotlight Search or a tap in the Control Center. Siri is much more helpful now too, and it’s always lurking nearby to help out. The grid of apps I’m so used to is mostly for emotional support at this point. I didn’t need a folding phone to learn that, but it helped. Above all, the new-notebook effect proved to be just as strong as always. The shiny new thing eventually fades into the background. You certainly don’t need a $2,000 phone to reevaluate your homescreen. You can — and I will continue to — just carry a little notebook around with your regular phone. A fun new gadget is delightful, don’t get me wrong. But don’t hang all your hopes and dreams for a new you on one of them. Photography by Allison Johnson / The Verge

articles.title: The HomeView and Echo Show 16 could be the family computers I’ve been asking for
articles.summary: Apple’s HomeView and Amazon’s Echo Show 16 aim to fix much of what was wrong with the smart display category. Except the price.
articles.body: Three years ago, I wrote an obituary for the smart display. The category — smart speakers with touchscreens attached — was stuck with a few underpowered gadgets from Google and Amazon that tried to do too much and did too little well. Back then, I also laid out what they needed to do to improve. This month, Apple and Amazon launched new smart displays that check nearly every box on that list. Based on my brief hands-on time with Apple’s first smart display, the $299 HomeView, and Amazon’s $499.99 Echo Show 16, a ground-up rebuild of its smart display line, these could finally turn the smart display into what it should have been all along: the family computer. Not a place to do homework or pay the bills, but a shared screen the whole household can use to check the calendar, see who’s at the door, and figure out what’s for dinner. [Image: Apple’s HomeView has a clean, simple interface. The biggest shift is that both companies have finally brought computer-class hardware to the space: Apple with its A18 chip (the same as in the MacBook Neo) and Liquid Retina display, and Amazon with a MediaTek processor and the same Nanomatte display as its new Alexa Tablet. This turns a category plagued by underpowered hardware and limited software into devices people might actually want to use. The catch is price. In 2023, the Echo Show 5 cost $85 and the Nest Hub $99. Apple’s HomeView, the cheaper of the two new models, costs three times that. But these devices now have a much clearer purpose, beyond being a vessel for each company’s revamped voice assistant. And with the software to back it up, they might actually be worth the investment. [Image: The Echo Show 16 offers a more tablet-style interface, with options for a calendar or a smart home dashboard. As our lives have become increasingly digital, the need for a central place to corral all the information required to run a busy household has only grown. For years, the calendar, grocery list, meal plan, and chores all lived inside one person’s phone, creating an exhausting mental load. Add in the connected home, and the need for a communal device grows even greater: an interface anyone in the house can use to check who is at the door without opening it, adjust the thermostat, or dim all the lights with a tap or a quick voice command. Yes, some devices can do some of these things, but none do them all well. The popularity of devices like the Skylight Calendar shows the need for a communal household screen. And while a tablet might seem like a natural fit, it has two challenges: limited multiuser support, and anything with a battery will wander into someone’s bedroom and die under a pillow. I learned that from personal experience. I thought Google’s Pixel Tablet, a hybrid tablet and smart display, was the category’s next evolution, though I wasn’t wild about its detachable screen. That turned out to be a big problem in my house — along with its half-baked smart home support. Google reportedly canceled its successor 18 months later. [Image: HomeView has some built-in apps, and it relies on your iPhone to run others. With their new devices, Apple and Amazon are bringing three things to the category that I’ve been wanting for years: computer-class hardware, a display built for sharing that can easily switch between users, and a screen that is always on and as easy to use as a light switch. No PIN to enter or screensaver to swipe away, just reach out and tap to control your lights or scroll through your calendar. Both the HomeView and Echo Show 16 appear to solve these problems. (Of course, I’ll need to test them properly to be sure.) However, that’s where the similarities end. What I find fascinating about these two side-by-side product launches is the different approach each company is taking to fit these devices into your household. Amazon has built one screen for the household that works without your phone — you don’t even need one to set it up (although it helps). Apple has built a screen that is an extension of your phone; it has communal features, but they’re limited compared with what you can do if you connect your phone. [Image: The Echo Show 16 has a new meal planning feature as part of its Family Management homescreen. The reason for the split is obvious: Apple is built around the iPhone; Amazon is built around, well, everything else. Apple’s approach treats the person as the user; HomeView is designed to know you. In Apple’s demo, Siri AI knew exactly when your friend would arrive at the front door from the airport based on reading your text messages and could turn on the coffee machine so their espresso was ready the moment they walked in. But while HomeView has communal features, most of the good stuff seems to appear only when HomeView recognizes your face and your phone is nearby. Amazon’s approach treats the household as the user; the Echo Show is designed to know your home. The company’s Omnisense technology built into its devices can sense presence, temperature, and room acoustics throughout your home. One of Amazon’s demos showed that when someone walks up your driveway, a figure appears on a map of your home, and you can tap it to see a live view of their approach through your Ring camera. While Amazon doesn’t have the same personal context as an iPhone, the Echo Show 16 offers broader features for the household, including meal planning, a full Fire TV, and a color-coded household calendar. Amazon is selling a maximal feature set at a premium price designed for everyone while Apple is pushing a more polished, narrower product at a lower price, aimed squarely at its existing users. I’m looking forward to seeing which approach works best once I have these devices in my home. But for the first time in years, I’m excited about testing a smart display. I guess my obituary was premature. Photography by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

articles.title: Waymo’s next robotaxi is a purpose-built Toyota bZ4X
articles.summary: Waymo and Toyota are partnering to build autonomous bZ4X robotaxis on the factory line in Japan, launching service in Tokyo in 2027 before expanding to the UK.
articles.body: Waymo announced today that it will use Toyota bZ4X electric vehicles that are assembled in Japan for a robotaxi service in Tokyo. The news builds on the strategic partnership between Waymo and Toyota which was first announced in April 2025. The robotaxis will be built entirely under one roof at Toyota’s Takaoka plant in Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture, Japan. Instead of building regular cars and modifying them later, the factory will install Waymo’s self-driving sensors and computers right on the assembly line as each car is made. A team-up between the world’s largest automaker and the world’s leader in autonomous driving obviously has huge implications. Currently, Waymo uses two vehicle models on the road today — the Jaguar I-Pace and Ojai based on the Zeekr RT — with a third based on the Hyundai Ioniq 5 set to deploy soon. By adding the bZ4X, Waymo is attempting to prove that its autonomous driving technology is compatible with a wide range of vehicle types. Waymo has long positioned itself as a software and systems supplier — the “Waymo Driver” — rather than an automaker. This also represents a shift in terms of how Waymo acquires and modifies the vehicles that end up in its fleet. Up until now, the company was doing things the hard way by buying a finished car from a factory, shipping it to a separate facility, and retrofitting it with sensors, computers, and extra wiring. The decision to build the sensor suite and compute into the bZ4X on Toyota’s own assembly line could help eliminate redundant labor, bespoke brackets, and secondary shipping — and possibly bring down costs for Waymo. Waymo says it will begin initial testing and validation in Japan starting next year. Following that, the new vehicles will roll out to the United Kingdom, in addition to other international markets, for robotaxi operations. Waymo also says it is continuing to explore integrating its technology into Toyota vehicles for personally owned autonomous vehicles. And the company is working with Woven by Toyota, the automaker’s software and mobility spinout, to use Waymo’s operational and safety telemetry to improve road safety across general vehicle fleets and traffic infrastructure.

articles.title: This electric screwdriver uses a camera and AI to figure out what bit you need
articles.summary: The Arrowspace S1 electric screwdriver has a camera on the end so a built-in AI model can figure out exactly which bit you need to tighten or loosen a screw.
articles.body: Companies like Hoto and Fanttik have elevated the design and functionality of tools like electric screwdrivers, but Arrowmax wants to make them smarter by adding a camera and AI that work together to eliminate the trial and error of finding the exact type and size of bit you need. It’s convenient, but also helpful, as choosing the wrong size could potentially leave you with a stripped screw and a much harder repair. Arrowmax is making the Arrowspace S1 available through a Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign, but the company has already successfully crowdfunded other products. You can preorder the screwdriver by itself for around $79, but its functionality and usefulness is expanded by bundling it with the S1 smart bit case that bumps the preorder price to around $129. Full retail pricing will be higher, and the S1 isn’t expected to ship until April 2027 at the earliest. On the bottom of the S1 is a small camera with an LED light that’s used to capture an image of a screw head. To ensure the screwdriver’s AI model has the best possible image to work with, next to the camera is a “precision contact probe” that extends and rests on the surface of the screw to ensure the camera is always at the ideal focus distance. [Media: Once the AI processes the photo, the type and size of bit you need will be displayed through a connected mobile app. Based on the identified screw, the screwdriver will also automatically select a safe torque setting to reduce the risk of damaging the fastener. To save you the trouble of having to find the exact bit that’s needed, the optional S1 Smart Case has a collection of 52 steel bits with an LED next to each one that lights up so the one you need is easy to spot. The Arrowspace S1 features a 600mAh rechargeable battery the company claims delivers enough power to run for up to 90 minutes, or tighten or loosen over 900 screws. That performance will vary if you turn off the automatic torque adjustments and increase it yourself. The remaining charge is displayed on the screwdriver’s OLED screen which also shows the current torque setting and which direction it’s set to rotate.

articles.body: As the weather cools, it may be worth investing in a smart thermostat to help lower your energy bills. Right now, Google’s fourth-gen Nest Learning Thermostat is on sale in all three colors for $219.99 ($60 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and The Home Depot, matching its best price of the year and just $10 shy of its all-time low. [Product: Google Nest Learning Thermostat (fourth-gen) | Google’s latest Nest Learning Thermostat is its most capable to date, and comes with new features designed to lower energy consumption without sacrificing comfort. Like prior models, it learns your heating and cooling preferences over time and automatically creates a schedule based on your habits, so you don’t have to constantly adjust the temperature yourself. It can also suggest schedule changes to save energy and automatically adjusts the temperature when you’re away. Additionally, it includes a remote temperature sensor in the box, so you can better adjust the temperature in your preferred room, whether that’s the bedroom or another space in your home. The Nest Learning Thermostat also improves on its predecessor with a beautifully designed adaptive display that shows your temperature settings, the weather, and the time from across the room. When you get closer, it reveals more detailed information, including outdoor air quality and humidity levels. The Matter-ready device also works with more HVAC systems than the third-gen model, along with a host of compatible humidifiers, dehumidifiers, and ventilation equipment. Plus, unlike many smart thermostats, it doesn’t require a C-wire in most homes either, though using one can help ensure consistent power. Read our full Nest Learning Thermostat (fourth-gen) review. articles.summary: Walmart’s budget-friendly Vizio TV features mini-LED backlighting and quantum dots, and can be configured to skip Vizio’s OS entirely.
articles.body: Modern smart TVs let you skip the streaming device, which is convenient, but they also come with their own issues, including privacy concerns and frequent updates. The Vizio Mini LED Quantum TV lets you cut out the rigamarole and just get straight to the HDMI ports. And right now, it’s discounted at Walmart, with the 65-inch model going for $358 ($40 off) and the 85-inch model going for $698 ($100 off). [Product: Vizio Mini LED Quantum TV | Although Vizio’s Mini LED TV comes loaded with Vizio OS, you can bypass the TV’s host of agreements during setup. By pushing past the manufacturer’s warnings about “missing out” on smart TV features, you can disable the built-in operating system, letting you use your own streaming device like a Roku or Apple TV 4K without worrying about what data Vizio and Walmart might be collecting. As for specs, the TV features quantum dots for full, vivid color and high brightness (our testing showed it can reach 936 nits when calibrated thanks to its mini-LED panel). There are some compromises, though, which is expected given the low price point. The IPS panel doesn’t have the best black levels, as you might see on more expensive sets, and there’s a touch of motion blur during faster scenes, which may also hurt its appeal for gamers. It also has three HDMI ports, but they’re only 2.0, although the screen only supports up to 4K at 60Hz, so it’s not detrimental to the experience. Read our full Vizio Mini LED Quantum TV review.

articles.title: Rivian’s autonomy gamble faces its first real test
articles.summary: Rivian is betting big on point-to-point hands-free driving, custom silicon, and robotaxis to rival Tesla’s FSD — even as rising tech costs threaten its R2 margins.
articles.body: During an hourlong earnings call last night, Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe spent less time talking about the production ramp of the all-important R2 SUV than he did hyping the company’s still-unproven autonomous vehicle ambitions. But the company faces a crucial test later this year, when it rolls out its point-to-point hands-free driving feature — first to its own employees for testing and validation in 2026, and later to customers in 2027. Following that, Rivian says it will launch its first robotaxi vehicles in partnership with Uber in 2028. In short, the next two years will determine whether Rivian will succeed or fail in its high-stakes quest to become a full-stack autonomy player. “We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator,” Derek Mulvey, VP for finance, said during the call. Success is not guaranteed. Tesla has a huge head start with its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) in over 1.7 million active customer cars. But trying to match Tesla’s driver-assist features — while simultaneously designing its own silicon chips, buying pricey sensors, and paying for massive AI computing power — is a huge financial gamble, especially while Rivian is still struggling to build and sell its mass-market R2 vehicles at scale. (The R2 recently became Rivian’s best-selling vehicle by volume, so progress continues.) "“We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator.”" - Derek Mulvey But it’s unclear whether Rivian sees the R2 as its make-or-break vehicle or if solving autonomy will be the true decider. That leaves the company in the middle of a difficult balancing act: launching an ambitious, mass-market electric vehicle while simultaneously reinventing itself as a full-stack autonomous driving powerhouse. Of course, the feature itself needs to work for Rivian to succeed. During the call, Scaringe revealed that he has been using the new point-to-point driving system in his own commute to the office every day, calling it “a wonderful” experience. He continued: > So, our view is that that is going to become a big driver of demand. And I think it’s unclear how quickly the whole — you know, the whole US market and the whole automotive market — starts to shift to really wanting this, and this being a major purchase criterion. But certainly, we’re at the front end of an inflection point where it’s more and more people exposed to what this could do… We do think it’s a really big driver, in the long term, for market share for us. But Scaringe was cagey about other details. When asked about Rivian’s take rate for its Autonomy Plus package — in other words, what percentage of Rivian buyers who purchase or subscribe to the software out of the total customer base — the chief executive declined to share the exact number. “The take rate on Autonomy Plus has exceeded our expectations,” he said, “and we’re quite encouraged by it.” Rivian’s execs are no doubt envious of Tesla’s take rates for FSD: Over 75 percent of new Tesla buyers in North America opted to get FSD in the third quarter of 2026, the company recently reported. Meanwhile, Rivian reported $605 million in revenue from software and subscription services in Q3 2026, a 45 percent increase year over year. And Rivian brought in $256 million in profit in software and services, up $102 million from last year, with a strong 42 percent profit margin. Rivian will likely spend more money than it brings in as it keeps buying expensive computers and AI systems. On the call, the company pointed out that computer chips, memory, and electronics are getting pricier. It also warned that adding two processors and costly lidar sensors to some R2 models could eat into the profits it hoped to make by building the vehicle in large numbers. The point-to-point system will face its own hurdles, including edge cases and the complexities of urban driving. A vehicle crash could damage Rivian’s brand and reputation, just as Tesla has experienced many times with FSD. And even though Rivian intends to roll out the feature to require active driver supervision, the company will likely face legal challenges when things inevitably go wrong. To be sure, Rivian couldn’t afford to sit on the sidelines and concede the autonomous crown to Tesla and Waymo. Self-driving tech could help Rivian post big, software-company-style profits, but paying for expensive AI development while also trying to build the R2 at scale makes the next year or two its riskiest period ever.

articles.title: My husband switched to a dumbphone for a month. Now he doesn't want his smartphone back.
articles.summary: Things feel lighter after living with the Light Phone III.
articles.body:
If you buy something through a link in this article, we may earn commission.

You know that panic you feel when you leave the house and realize you don't have your phone? Have you ever wondered if that feeling is a little unhealthy ? I have. No, we can't call or text anyone, and we could get physically lost without a digital map in our pocket — but rarely are those situations truly dire. So I have to wonder where the panic comes from.

I'm not the only one who suspects it stems from addiction. We look at our phones for hours every day. They send us between 50 and 200 notifications daily, depending on which survey you read, and those pings can induce a flight-or-flight stress response and increase our addiction levels .

I've tried a few options to help me curb my phone's hold on me and so far my favorite is the Light Phone III . That said, this device isn't something you can adopt without a few considerations — and a lot of adjustment.

This phone is a purpose-built, pared-down, intentionally "dumb" phone. It has all the features that most would consider useful tools (texting, phone calls, GPS directions), but it lacks the things that suck you in and monopolize your attention (web browser, social media, streaming).

After using it for a week or so, I saw its potential — but as a tech reporter, I couldn't abandon my (multiple) smartphones to make it my daily driver. (How would I talk to Siri ?) So, as I often do in the course of testing, I brought my family into the mix. My husband, Brandon, replaced his Samsung phone with the Light Phone III for a full month and allowed me to grill him periodically on the experience. The verdict: he doesn't want to give it up, but there remain some pain points.

As I suspected, Brandon also found the Light Phone to be a soul-calming return to a time before the digital onslaught . But not at first. After transferring his number to the Light Phone (done fairly easily on a computer), he ran into a wall of frustration. With no browser or apps, he lost access to all the world's knowledge, which we are very used to having in our pockets. Want to know where you saw the lead actress from the Backrooms before? You now have to wait until you get home to your desk-tethered computer to learn it was that lovely Norwegian indie film .

While the world moves forward on smartphones that can identify insects and house AI agents that make weekend plans for you, you're mired in ignorance when you use something like the Light Phone III. Beyond idle question-answering, you also have nothing to look at as you wait for things. Unless you're participating in a rapid-fire text thread, you have no reason to stare at your dumbphone while you wait for your food at the taco truck or stand in line at the coffee shop. You have to, as Brandon put it, "fully experience waiting in waiting rooms again."

Possibly the most frustrating part is that the rest of the world just assumes you have a smartphone. When a restaurant replaces its menu with a QR code, you have to ask the hostess to hunt down a paper version — like you're a child or time traveller from 2010. Parking lots all but require you to pay for your spot with your phone nowadays. And when Brandon shopped for supplies at the art store, the cashier gave him a concerned look when he explained he had no way of accessing the digital coupon that could save him substantial money. (She graciously gave him the discount anyway.)

Brandon says it took about two weeks for the frustration to subside. Once that happened, a lightness, or a calmness, came over him. If you get the sense that I'm speaking in vaguely spiritual terms, you're not wrong. The Light Phone comes with a little paper 'zine (which spoke to the grungy GenX hearts in both Brandon and I), and it conveys an emotional, motivational and very philosophical breakdown of the lost attention and missed experiences that result from our smartphone addictions. A lot is taken from us, everyday, by the little glowing screens in our pockets. Getting that back can feel a little magical.

Not being able to immediately look stuff up? Brandon says if it's important, he'll remember to look it up when he gets home. If he forgets, it must not have been that important. (Most things are not that important.) There are workarounds that let you deal with the world's assumption that you have a smartphone, even if it requires a little initial discomfort. And being distractionless in dull situations is undoubtedly boring, but also likely good for our brains .

The best thing the Light Phone brought, however, is the loss of that panic I mentioned above. "The muscle memory goes away," says Brandon, "the impulse to reach for your phone disappears. After a while, I forget I'm carrying it." I can confirm: We had a few friends over and one of them asked to see his dumbphone. Brandon walked to the shelf where he usually keeps it before realizing it had been in his pocket all night without him realizing it. As someone who is acutely aware of their phone's location like it's a newborn baby, this blew me away.

Brandon still has his old smartphone. It mostly stays at home, but he does take it with him occasionally. He needs it for mundane things, like when he ships packages through the post office. Instead of messing with our temperamental printer, he takes the smartphone with the shipping label's QR code to the P.O.

He also uses his smartphone like an old-school iPod, downloading playlists from Qobuz so he can listen to music in the car. This workaround isn't strictly necessary, as the Light Phone III does have a music player and a Bluetooth connection, but Brandon hasn't yet felt the need to go through the MP3 downloading process.

Other things — like directions, the morning alarm and notes functions — all work just fine. You can take, send and receive pictures with the Light Phone III, too, though the lack of modern hardware and software features mean your photos will never look like they came from a pro camera. But what's really lost here? When I send Brandon a cute picture of our cute dog, he sees the cuteness. When he sends me a snapshot of that same dog, I, too, register the cuteness.

Ultimately, using the Light Phone means "you have to think ahead," Brandon says, "and accept that all knowledge is not at your fingertips." You might have to wait to look something up — or you might realize that looking that thing up isn't actually important at all.

articles.title: Jessica Lange Thinks Her Acting Career Is About Over: ‘Maybe It’s Not a Bad Way to End’
articles.summary: Jessica Lange thinks her acting career might be coming to a close.
articles.body:
Jessica Lange thinks her acting career might be coming to a close.

In a new interview with Rolling Stone , Lange was asked about what projects were next up for her after "American Horror Story" Season 13. In response, the actress was candid about the fact that there may not be many more roles in her future.

"I actually feel like I'm coming to an end," Lange said. "Maybe it's not a bad way to end, that last film being 'Long Day's Journey Into Night' and playing Mary Tyrone. There are a couple projects that have been in the works forever that may or may not happen. I don't know. It doesn't seem easy to get things made anymore. At least not the kind of films that interest me."

When asked how she'd want to be remembered if her acting career did indeed come to a close, Lange was quick with an answer.

"For some good parts. For some good films. For being an honest actor," she said. "I've been incredibly lucky. I love acting, and I've had decades of being able to do it, which has been a joy for me. Difficult at times, balancing family and career and locations and dragging my kids here and there. But it all was a great adventure. I'm so grateful that [it] came my way."

Fans of the Oscar winner have been loving her return to Ryan Murphy's FX horror anthology series this year. After stepping away from "AHS" for a few years after becoming a staple of the franchise, Lange returned for "13" along with a number of the biggest names from past seasons. She even reprised four of her former roles from past seasons, which is what finally got her to come back.

"Why I said yes to this season was the idea of revisiting, reprising these four roles," Lange shared. "Because when we originally did them, it was just so new and crazy and wild. There was so much to do with every single episode that it was a wonderful adventure. Working with really what was a repertory company — all of the actors returning every season and creating a new character in a new story in a new situation — it was a wonderful way to work. I loved it."

articles.title: Exclusive details about Akai’s MPC Sample Key
articles.summary: An exclusive first look at the open-source MPC Sample Key reveals it will focus on pitched sample playback rather than chopping up drum breaks.
articles.body: Akai teased its new MPC Sample Key on Instagram earlier this week, and said it plans to open-source its software so the modding community can hack it to their hearts’ delight. While there’s no word yet on when the device will launch or how much it will cost, The Verge has received exclusive images of the upcoming instrument that offer some details about its feature set. While the Sample Key shares many of the same controls as the MPC Sample — including the three context-sensitive encoders, a large main encoder — it seems designed for pitched sample playback, rather than chopping up drums. In fact, the “chop” button from the MPC Sample is missing entirely from the Sample Key. The dedicated pitch and mod wheels are another clue there. But there are also buttons for changing the octave range of the 25-key keyboard, as well as ones labeled “chord” and “arp.” Presumably, those enable a chord playback mode and an arpeggiator. While using an arpeggiator to play back drum samples can be a fun way to create rhythms, it’s more commonly used for melodic and bass parts. And a chord mode would be basically useless for drums. Those options also appear to replace the chop function from the standard MPC Sample. [Image: [Image: [Image: There also appears to be a dedicated looper that could be useful for live performance and layering sounds. And, instead of the Flex Beat effects from the original MPC Sample, there’s something called “Swarm.” Though what that is isn’t exactly clear at the moment. Like the first entry in the Sample series, the Key has a built-in mic and speaker for all-in-one music production. While we haven’t gotten a glimpse at the back panel yet, the config options on the front suggest that, in addition to MIDI, the Sample Key will have CV outs for integrating with modular synths. Correction October 30th: The MPC Sample Key is 25 keys, not 37.

articles.title: Elon Musk's Starlink could be your next cellphone carrier
articles.summary: SpaceX is reportedly pursuing access to 80,000 cell sites to turn Starlink into a major wireless carrier rivaling Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile.
articles.body: Ever look at your cellphone bill and wonder why you're paying so much when you still can't get a decent signal? Maybe calls drop inside your house or your phone loses service during a road trip. It's frustrating, especially when the big wireless companies keep promising better coverage. Now, Elon Musk wants to give you another option. His company, SpaceX, is reportedly pursuing access to at least 80,000 cell sites across the United States. The goal is to turn Starlink into a major wireless carrier that could compete directly with Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile. If Musk pulls this off, the way you choose your cellphone service could change. Join our CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us today, Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com. Missed this morning’s live class? Register at CyberGuyLive.com to watch the replay. AMAZON LEO SATELLITE INTERNET TAKES ON STARLINK SpaceX wants 80,000 cell sites across America SpaceX is reportedly negotiating with major cellular infrastructure companies to secure access to at least 80,000 sites nationwide. One company reportedly involved is Crown Castle, which owns and operates roughly 40,000 cell towers across the country. During an Oct. 21 earnings call, Crown Castle CEO Chris Hillabrant was asked about potential leasing discussions with SpaceX and other satellite providers. His response was revealing. "You can assume that we're talking to all parties," he said, although he declined to discuss specific customers. That's a significant development. Cell towers provide the infrastructure that keeps our phones connected across the country. Wireless companies typically lease space on these towers rather than build every structure themselves. That approach helps them expand coverage without taking on the full cost of owning the infrastructure. For perspective, the Wireless Infrastructure Association counted about 158,500 purpose-built cell towers nationwide in 2025. SpaceX's reported target of 80,000 cell sites would represent a substantial expansion, although cell sites and physical towers are not the same thing. A single tower can support equipment from multiple wireless networks, so the two figures are not directly comparable. Still, the reported discussions remain preliminary. SpaceX has not publicly confirmed agreements covering those 80,000 sites. Why Elon Musk needs cell towers when Starlink has satellites Here's something you might be wondering. If Starlink already has satellites orbiting Earth, why does SpaceX need thousands of cell towers? The answer comes down to how wireless coverage works. Satellites can provide connectivity in remote areas where traditional cell towers are scarce. However, signals from space can struggle to reach phones inside buildings or in places with an obstructed view of the sky. That's where ground-based cellular networks come in. Traditional towers can provide stronger, more consistent service in areas where satellite connections face limitations. By combining both technologies, SpaceX hopes to create a network that keeps people connected across more locations. There's another interesting piece to the strategy. SpaceX has also discussed adding small cellular base stations to equipment installed at Starlink customers' homes and businesses. Those stations could help provide mobile coverage without requiring the company to rely entirely on traditional cell towers. However, there's a catch. Starlink customers install their equipment where they need home internet. Those locations may not line up with where a nationwide cellphone network needs additional coverage. That's why access to established cellular infrastructure could prove so valuable. FCC CHAIRMAN CARR SAYS SPECTRUM AUCTION WILL MAKE WIRELESS FASTER, CHEAPER WHILE RAISING BILLIONS FOR TREASURY Starlink Mobile takes another major step forward SpaceX has already made several investments that support its wireless ambitions. On October 8, investment firm Grain Management announced an agreement to sell its nationwide portfolio of 800 MHz wireless spectrum to SpaceX. The deal remains subject to Federal Communications Commission approval. If you're unfamiliar with spectrum, think of it as the radio frequencies that carry wireless signals between your phone and a network. Different frequencies have different strengths. Lower-frequency signals generally travel farther and penetrate buildings more effectively than higher-frequency signals. That could help Starlink Mobile deliver coverage in places where satellite connections alone might struggle. SpaceX also received FCC authorization in October to deploy a new constellation of up to 15,000 direct-to-device satellites. These satellites are designed to communicate with compatible phones and support a broader range of mobile services. However, that authorization doesn't mean all the satellites are already operating. Together, those developments help explain why Musk is getting serious about the wireless business. SpaceX is assembling the pieces needed to connect phones through satellites and ground-based networks. During SpaceX's October earnings call, Musk said the company would expand its terrestrial networks to provide broader connectivity wherever SpaceX and Starlink are permitted to operate. He also said satellite launches and spectrum acquisitions would help Starlink Mobile become a major U.S. wireless carrier. Could Starlink really challenge Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile? The possibility has already caught Wall Street's attention. Following reports of SpaceX's cell tower negotiations, shares of major wireless companies fell on October 23. Meanwhile, cellular infrastructure companies saw their shares rise as investors anticipated potential business from SpaceX. But entering the wireless market won't come cheap. Analysts at TD Cowen reportedly estimated that building a nationwide terrestrial network could cost more than $80 billion. The process could take years, even for a company with SpaceX's financial resources. And SpaceX would face established competitors with decades of experience. Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile already operate extensive networks. They also have millions of customers and established retail operations. Interestingly, SpaceX already works with T-Mobile through its T-Satellite with Starlink service. That partnership allows compatible phones to connect to satellites in certain areas without traditional cellular coverage. So, Musk's company currently helps support a wireless provider it could eventually compete against. That's an unusual position, but it also gives SpaceX experience delivering satellite connectivity to everyday phones. If Starlink Mobile becomes a standalone carrier, customers could eventually have another nationwide option beyond today's three dominant providers. When could Starlink Mobile become available? If you're already wondering when you can switch, there's an important detail to keep in mind. SpaceX has not announced a confirmed launch date for a fully independent nationwide cellphone service. The company expects to begin deploying its next-generation Starlink Mobile satellites in 2027. However, building a terrestrial cellular network presents a separate challenge. SpaceX still needs access to suitable tower locations and the equipment required to operate them. The company also faces additional regulatory requirements. Its nationwide spectrum agreement with Grain Management, for example, still needs FCC approval. Meanwhile, expanding coverage across the country will take considerable time. Even with thousands of satellites overhead, SpaceX would need a carefully planned ground network to deliver a reliable alternative to existing carriers. For now, Starlink's existing satellite partnerships should not be confused with the proposed nationwide cellphone service. What this means to you If you've been frustrated with your cellphone bill or unreliable coverage, another major wireless provider could eventually give you more options. More competition could mean better wireless deals. Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile may face pressure to improve their plans if SpaceX introduces an appealing alternative. However, Starlink Mobile has not announced pricing for a standalone nationwide service. There's no guarantee it will cost less than what you're paying today. Coverage could be the bigger selling point. By combining satellites with traditional cell towers, SpaceX could potentially reach places where existing wireless networks struggle. That could be especially appealing if you live in a rural community or frequently travel through areas with weak signals. However, actual performance will depend on where SpaceX installs its equipment and how well its satellite connections work. The real test will come when SpaceX reveals its pricing and coverage plans. Can Starlink offer better service in places where other carriers struggle? And will it give people a compelling reason to switch? Those answers will determine whether Musk's wireless ambitions actually benefit cellphone customers. GOV JEFF LANDRY: SPACEX BETS ON LOUISIANA AS AMERICA’S NEXT FRONTIER TAKES OFF IN THE SOUTH Kurt's key takeaways I've been covering wireless technology long enough to know that big promises don't always translate into better cellphone service. We've heard plenty about expanding coverage and improving connectivity. Yet there are still places where you can barely make a call. That's why I find SpaceX's plans interesting. Combining satellites with traditional cellular infrastructure could eventually give people more options, particularly in areas where the big carriers have struggled. At the same time, I'm curious about the bigger picture. Musk already has an enormous satellite network, and now he reportedly wants to build a major wireless business on the ground. That could introduce some welcome competition. However, I'd like to know what the pricing will look like and whether Starlink can provide reliable coverage where people actually use their phones. If it can deliver on those promises, the established carriers may have a serious reason to worry. And frankly, a little more competition in the cellphone business wouldn't hurt. If Elon Musk offered you cellphone service through Starlink, would you trust his company enough to leave Verizon, AT&T or T-Mobile? Or would you rather stick with the wireless provider you already know? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com Sign up for my FREE CyberGuy Newsletter CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Copyright 2026 CyberGuy.com. All rights reserved.
