articles.body: Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 150, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, happy Halloween, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.) This week, I was in the Smoky Mountains in Tennessee on a family vacation. It was delightful (and the reason this week’s Installer is a little short). I’ve also been reading about job hunting and 30 Rock and crypto detectives, testing the DuckDuckGo browser after a bunch of you told me to add it to the list, watching the adorable new Pixar short over and over, getting caught up on VisionQuest, playing with my new Pebble Index 01 now that it finally arrived, listening to music on my rad-looking new CMF Speaker S, and eating a worrying number of pumpkin chocolate chip muffins. I also have for you some new gear from Apple and Amazon, a better way to read books on your phone, a resurrected note-taking app, an absurdly expensive robovac, and much more. Let’s do it. (As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What are you watching / reading / listening to / playing / giving to trick-or-treaters this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.) The Drop * The new iPad Mini. With apologies to the touchscreen iMac, this is the most intriguing new Apple product of the week. I, too, am annoyed that there’s no ProMotion screen, but I’m excited about thinner and lighter, and I’m very excited about the idea of a functionally water- and dustproof tablet. * The Alexa Photo Frame. The Echo Show 16 is a cool smart home hub, but $500 is just too much for me. But a $200 digital photo frame that is also, sometimes, only when you need it, a smart home hub and timer-setter? That will end up in my living room. And my parents’. And my in-laws’. * nvAlt. One of the all-time great note-taking apps got its first update in forever, and now it can run on modern Macs. (The developer is also working on nvUltra, which is in beta and even better.) If you’re a plain-text notetaker, you’re gonna want to get back into this app. * Chromagraph. The director Rian Johnson — yes, that one — worked with his favorite cinematographer to make it possible to process iPhone photos the way they like best. An extremely opinionated camera app from people who have very much earned those opinions. I love it. * “I love the iPod. It ruined everything.” This Mic The Snare video is both a very good history of the iPod and a surprisingly cogent theory that the iPod is to blame for some of the worst things about modern life. I still miss my gold iPod Mini. * Readwise Books. A really nice-looking, really powerful app for buying, reading, and tracking your books. Right now it’s a little bit “better Kindle” and a lot “better Goodreads.” So far I’m mostly using the social feed to get recommendations from strangers, which suits me just fine. This went right onto my Boox Palma homescreen. * Phantom Blade Zero. Currently burning up the Steam charts, this one. People love the martial arts-inspired combat system and the game’s overall aesthetic, and I’m even hearing good things about the music. * No Man’s Sky. This is definitely one of the biggest and most ambitious games to ever come to iOS (and all it took was a decade!). It works on pretty much all recent iPhones and iPads, too. Just don’t be fooled by the Free sign at the top; the game costs $20. But it’s worth it. * The Matic Serene. Two things here. One, $1,700 is an absolutely ludicrous price for a robot vacuum, no matter how good it is. Two, “we made it quieter” is maybe the quickest way to get me in particular to want your robot vacuum. Please, friends, do not let me buy this. Crowdsourced Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky. “Currently watching: VisionQuest. It’s quite good! James Spader has really stolen the show, but I am a little biased as a huge Blacklist fan.” — Spencer “I’m using CallMe to coordinate when my friends and I call each other. You can tap ‘I’m free for the next 15/30/60 minutes’ and your friends will get a notification. When you’re both free you can call each other (outside of the app). Makes it easy to reconnect.” — Jordan “I’ve been spending the last few days working on my Top 10 for WXPN’s annual Top 885. This year is ‘Top 885 Songs from Movies and TV,’ and it’s especially challenging.” — Ben “The one game that I play religiously is Clues By Sam, a daily logic puzzle game where speed and accuracy is the goal. Because everyone starts at the same spot, your time is your score, and it’s very fun competing with friends every day. Puzzles range from easy (~2 minutes) on Mondays to Brutal (up to ~15 minutes) on Sundays. Would 100% recommend adding it to your daily rotation.” — Adam “Maybe niche, but Steam Frame and trying out older 3D media on it that flopped or became obsolete. Stereoscopic 3DS games and 3D movies work better than they ever did on original hardware, on devices with a dedicated individual display for each eye.” — Mango “I am sooo into the Vivaldi browser now, with the look and feel, and all the customisations! 😍” — Oscar “Spending some more time learning about the AT Protocol for a class project. The tech is neat. Fell down the rabbit hole of mental poker cryptography.” — James “The YouTube channel Digging the Greats by Brandon Shaw is fantastic for music lovers like myself. He deeply analyzes albums and songs in long-form videos, from Prince’s ‘Purple Rain’ to Kendrick Lamar’s To Pimp a Butterfly. I also recently finished two of a four-part video series: one where he only listened to music on an iPod for a month, and another where he explored the history of cassettes and mixtapes. I highly recommend checking out his channel if you love music!” — Josh “The Dark Matter finale is this week.” — Steve “I used Firefox for a long time but really don’t like their stance on AI and all the junk they keep adding (VPN, for instance). So I went to Librewolf, which is a Firefox fork that strips out all of the telemetry and AI and also pre-configures a bunch of hardening. I’ve encountered no problems whatsoever with any websites or streaming content.” — Nicholas Signing off Back in the day, before I worked in the basement and actually left my house on occasion, I had a real weakness for laptop bags. Even now, I have absolutely no need for a new one, but after watching Byron Seven’s video about designing a laptop sleeve / desk organizer / backpack thing, I desperately want the one he made. Even if you don’t want the product, watch the video — it’s a cool look into product design and just a fabulously made video about a bag. See you next week!

articles.title: I took two iPhones on vacation. The Duo won me over. | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The iPhone Duo has its frustrations, but it’s also fun and engaging enough that I didn’t want to switch back to my Pro Max.
articles.body:
“I think I’m going to switch back to my other iPhone.”

I’ll admit, I said this multiple times during my five-day vacation with the new iPhone Duo, after encountering frustrations with broken apps, unfamiliar gestures (a return to Touch ID, argh !), and camera concerns that had me lugging around two phones.

By the time the trip was over, I didn’t want to go back.

When I first unboxed the Duo, a loaner from Apple, I was genuinely intrigued. I felt a flutter of anticipation as I peeled back the factory seal wrap and booted up the device. In retrospect, this was probably the first signal that Duo was going to ultimately win me over.

As a tech reporter, I’ve received a lot of test devices over the years, so unfortunately, opening a package with a new gadget inside is no longer the thrill it used to be. But sometime in the days leading up to the Duo’s ship date, I found myself actually wanting one – I had started doing the math and comparing upgrade options that would allow me to afford the $2K the phone would cost. I started scrolling TikTok reviews of Duo cases . I hesitated not only because of the price but because moving to the Duo is a major change – especially coming from an iPhone 17 Pro Max. The phones could not be more different.

As I was about to head out on vacation when the Duo arrived, I decided to tote my 17 Pro Max with me too, as something of a safety net. I ended up using the Duo more, and grew comfortable with it over the course of the trip, despite some frustrations.

There’s always a psychological switching cost in changing phones, but particularly going from a high-end phone to a more experimental device like the Duo. For someone used to the iPhone’s long-perfected tech and thin rectangular shape, the Duo’s short, squat, and decidedly novel nature was somewhat off-putting at first.

“Where is all that screen real estate I used to have?” I lamented. “Will this thing even fit comfortably in my pocket?”

As it turns out, it does. Front and back pockets, in fact. Even while wearing a case. You can sit down with it in your back pocket, effectively squashing it, and it does not break. (I meant to be more careful, but I forgot to be, repeatedly, as I tend to carry phones in my back pocket when walking around. I sat on the phone countless times. It’s clearly not that fragile.)

I also dropped the phone (by accident!) at least three times. Twice from about table height and once when it got pushed off the side of the bed. It did not fall on soft carpet, but rather on concrete, tile, and wood floors. It didn’t break then either, and the screen didn’t crack. I wouldn’t call these professional drop tests by any means, but it certainly was a relief for someone fairly clumsy with their phone.

Of course, I did encounter some frustrations. I had to scroll more to read back through text threads because of the Duo’s small outer screen; unoptimized apps with numerous controls sometimes had key features tucked away in a “more” (three-dot) menu, leading to a hunt to find the option you needed; and, on multiple occasions, the Google Search app just froze.

Though not Apple’s fault, the latter turned out to be my biggest annoyance software-wise, given that Search is one of my go-to apps especially when traveling. On vacation, I open the app repeatedly to look up points of interest, restaurant reviews, distances between towns, weather, and more. But Google’s app would just stop working, and tapping its back button did nothing.

This seemed to be a problem specific to the Search app’s AI Mode, which these days you’re often dropped into without actually requesting it. (Even more reason to be annoyed by AI Search!) The workaround has been to force-close the app, so the next time you open it, your returned to the home screen with the search box. (It amazes me that, in a time when Google is facing a search decline because of AI, it wouldn’t have prioritized making its Search app functional on Apple’s latest device!)

In addition, many of the early reviews pointed out how many apps were not updated or redesigned for Duo at launch, which meant they had a telltale black bar on the side, cramping the limited screen real estate when the phone is closed even further. This is true, but personally speaking, I didn’t think it was a dealbreaker for making a switch to the Duo.

For one thing, companies have been pushing out their Duo-optimized updates fairly quickly. Those that have not – and there are still more than a few! – continue to be usable. They’re just kind of … ugly.

Google Maps was not Duo-optimized during the trip, yet I had no problem using it for driving directions, local search and discovery, route planning, and the like. If anything, the black-barred apps felt more like an aesthetic issue than a functional problem, even though they’re smaller than usual when the Duo is folded.

I expect all the major apps will eventually update. As for the older apps that never do? Well, it’s probably time to move on from apps no longer being maintained, I’d say, particularly in an era when older software is being exploited left and right by AI-enabled hacking tools.

However, I will agree with the other reviewers who complained about the lack of Face ID.

This is the Duo’s biggest drawback – not the screen, not the camera, not the lack of an Action button for launching your preferred AI assistant. It’s Touch ID.

It is much easier to look at your phone than to fiddle around with finger presses. While I easily avoided the need to use Touch ID to unlock the device – I am almost always wearing an Apple Watch, which serves as an alternative authentication method – I often stumbled when it came to using apps and Apple Pay.

Tap-and-pay is one of the areas where it’s immediately obvious how much smoother Face ID has made everyday tasks. Returning to Touch ID at the time of payment was cumbersome, given that you’re often holding shopping bags, a purse, and, in my case, a dog leash, in addition to the phone you’re using to pay with.

There’s a certain amount of what I guess I’ll call “muscle memory” that you have to overcome when you switch back to Touch ID. I found the easiest grip was to cradle the phone in your hand and use your thumb to authenticate. But where I repeatedly messed up was remembering to keep my thumb or finger on the Touch ID sensor long enough to authenticate. At times, my finger wasn’t situated quite right (I blame the dog pulling on the leash!), and I had to readjust. “I miss Face ID!,” I complained multiple times at checkout.

Though returning to Touch ID was something I got used to, it’s far from ideal. I can see this as being a real stopping point for some early adopters who would otherwise want to move to the Duo. It’s not an insurmountable problem, but it’s among the top reasons not to get the Duo now, in my opinion. (A future version is said to support Face ID .)

Another reason to be wary of the Duo? The camera. Much has been said about the Duo’s lesser camera system. The Duo has two rear cameras to my iPhone 17 Pro Max’s three. It has no telephoto lens. It has a 10x digital zoom versus the Pro’s 40x. The Pro has more advanced hardware for low-light photography and supports ProRAW, ProRes, and other advanced features.

Very simply put: if you are an iPhone photographer or a content creator, you shouldn’t consider the Duo as your primary device.

For, you know, us normal folks, the Duo’s camera is okay. Not great, but fine. What were you going to do with those photos you’re snapping anyway? Post them to Instagram Stories or Facebook? Text them to a friend? Look back on them fondly when they reappear in your photo widget on your Home Screen? Turn them into a Lock Screen wallpaper? None of these things requires a Pro-level camera.

Below are a few photos shot with the Duo versus others shot with the 17 Pro Max. None of the photos are using any special settings or filters; they are intentionally just average, non-professional point-and-shoot shots. Among my complaints are that the Duo’s image processing can, at times, make fine details, like the leaves on trees, look overprocessed. Meanwhile, distant landscapes can appear flatter or smoothed over — though, to be fair, the Blue Ridge Mountains are naturally hazy, so it’s hard to say how much of that is the camera. (Shots from the mountaintop were in low-light conditions — it was getting dark out.)

As for why to get the phone? This one’s easy; it’s a foldable . From Apple . First, foldables are whimsical in a way that slab phones will never be. They are toys for grown-ups! Developers are also clearly having fun building for the new format , so there are lots of new apps to play with. Plus, it’s a great way to watch movies, particularly with that Duo Folio case with a kickstand.

Second, it’s a foldable from Apple . The company has taken its time to get it right, which comes through in the details, from the barely visible crease to the consistent aspect ratio between screens, allowing content to scale proportionally. It’s also a foldable in Apple’s software ecosystem, which matters for those who move between Apple devices and services and who use and pay for apps that are designed for iOS specifically.

But here’s a small confession: in day-to-day life, I didn’t unfold the Duo as much as I thought I would. (To be clear: I absolutely did unfold it! I just thought I would do it more!)

There are two reasons for this. One: unfolding the device in public invites conversation, and it feels sort of like a flex; I’m not always in a place where I have time to chat. I expect this problem to diminish in time as the novelty wears off.

That said, I still had roughly half a dozen conversations with strangers while I was on vacation, from fellow shoppers to servers to business owners. I even handed them the device at times (when they couldn’t easily run off with it!) and let them fold and unfold it. One person wanted to see the Kid Cue feature in particular, which displays playful Snoopy animations on the phone’s outer display to get children to look toward the camera when you take their picture. They were genuinely delighted by this.

Anecdotally, the consensus was that the unfolded screen was something of a marvel to most: “You can’t see the hinge!” “Is that a screen protector or is it just like that?” (The inner screen has a matte, nano-texture finish, reducing glare. Once explained, it was also praised as “pretty cool.” )

“What if you get sand in it?,” a former Samsung Galaxy Fold owner asked. Their older Android foldable had been ruined after a trip to the beach where sand got into the hinge, causing damage to the screen. (This was not uncommon at the time.) The Duo is rated IP68, the “6” signifying higher dust resistance, making it dust-tight. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 was rated IP48, by comparison. I’m not expecting it will have the same issues, though I do hope a reviewer takes it to the beach soon!

I am certain that at least one of the handful of strangers I spoke to had never actually seen a phone that folded before. The fact that Apple has now made one means this concept will no longer be niche; it will be known to the mainstream.

The other reason I didn’t unfold it as much as I thought is that doing so feels like the start of a more intentional screen time session. When I do unfold the phone now, it’s because I’m truly engaging with what I’m doing on the phone, like watching a show on Netflix or dragging two apps side-by-side in split-screen mode for multitasking. (I love reading news in Inoreader and having X open off to the side to see what people are saying about the news, but that’s a use case that won’t apply to everyone!)

The split-screen feature is easy to use, too – with the app open, you swipe up from the bottom, then drag it to the left or right edge. Target boxes on each side help you visualize where it can move to, which is helpful. (You can also long-press on an app icon to open a split view, but I don’t do this as much.)

But as something of a “mini” phone in terms of screen size when closed, I’m somehow less drawn to what I think of as time-wasting apps like TikTok, Instagram, or casual games.

I’ve been thinking about this, and I don’t believe it’s just the lack of screen real estate when the phone is folded, or the fact that vertical apps haven’t been designed for the Duo’s unfolded landscape screen. Those concerns make sense from a practical, usability standpoint, of course, but there’s something more to this behavioral change, I believe.

For years, phones have been getting bigger , taller , thinner , and more comfortable to hold. Consequently, they easily sucked us into their digital worlds. With the Duo, the design seems to interrupt the way smartphones effortlessly pull us in, begging us to open apps and scroll endlessly.

Rather, the Duo feels like a device you open and use when you have reason to do so, not something you reflexively turn to when you’re bored or have a few minutes to spare. Because the best app use cases are when the phone is unfolded, and unfolding is something you do with careful consideration (and careful hands!), device use becomes more thoughtful.

This is not a bad thing. It also aligns with the embrace of retro tech already underway, where knobs and dials and buttons make engaging with technology feel more deliberate.

And for that reason, despite its faults, the Duo won me over. It’s a phone that’s compelling and fun — a phone I enjoyed picking up, but also found easier to put down.

articles.title: Best Buy is bundling a $100 gift card with touchscreen MacBook Pro preorders
articles.summary: Apple’s new touch-enabled MacBook Pro with a PROLED XDR display is available for preorder, and Best Buy will toss in a $100 gift card with your preorder.
articles.body: While the new touch-enabled MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR screen is available for preorder across a few major retailers, Best Buy is sweetening the deal by including a $100 gift card. The gift card will be automatically added to your cart when you preorder one of Apple’s highest-end laptops available in 14- or 16-inch configurations, and even one of its 14-inch MacBook Pro laptops with the M6 chip. You can verify that it’s been added to your order in the “Complete your purchase” section of the checkout page. [Product: Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display | My colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto got a chance to check out the new laptop at Apple’s event, and came away impressed by the Tandem OLED panel’s brightness and contrast, but described the update as “kind of boring” given the relatively small changes to the system otherwise. There are some unique changes to macOS that help make the new touch experience smoother, like magnifying the traffic light-colored buttons on windows when you move your finger near them. The PROLED laptops are also a bit thinner and lighter than standard models, and the Apple logo on the back glows like on older versions. Read our MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display hands-on.

articles.title: Windows 11 tries new shortcuts for Xbox gaming mode and search
articles.summary: The latest Windows Insider builds revamp search with filters, actions, and phone controls.
articles.body: The latest Windows 11 Insider build adds some powerful new search features and quick settings while in Xbox mode. The Xbox shortcuts let you control things like Bluetooth, WiFi, and power settings without having to exit gaming mode. The search improvements are quite comprehensive. You can now filter results for files, actions, or web results. You can also use the search box to perform actions like changing the screen brightness or volume, and even perform actions on a connected phone, including making calls. Results can also offer much more detail, like when a file was last modified and its author, or pull in charts for stock prices and weather forecasts. And you can train Windows 11 search by clicking inline thumbs-up or thumbs-down icons to help it improve over time. For the full list of changes, check out Microsoft’s blog post. Beta Build 26220.9836 and Experimental Build 26340.9843 are both available now to Windows Insiders.

articles.title: Jessica Biel Teases Bold New Direction for “7th Heaven” Reboot with No ‘Limitations’
articles.summary: Biel, who played Mary Camden in the original series, is set to produce the reboot
articles.body:
Jessica Biel says the 7th Heaven reboot will address technology, bullying, substance use and school pressures facing modern families

The original series ran for 11 seasons from 1996 to 2007, with Biel playing Mary Camden

Biel hopes to create realistic family viewing that includes faith, community and a more hopeful perspective

Jessica Biel is teasing a few of the changes to the 7th Heaven reboot.

During a recent episode of Collider Ladies Night , the 44-year-old actress shared an update on the series, which is in early development at CBS Studios.

"What we want to create, how we want to modernize it, is really the things that are happening for teenagers and families that have teenagers all the way down to the youngest child — technology-based issues, school stuff, bullying stuff, drugs, alcohol," Biel shared.

"All of those things we want to address in a very real way, which is, I think, what the original kind of gently touched on, but we were very careful about what our audience wanted. We had a lot of limitations. We have less limitations now," she added.

Biel starred in the initial series, which ran for 11 seasons, as Mary Camden from 1996 to 2007. The series — centered on a Protestant minister and his wife, and the challenges they faced raising seven children — also starred Stephen Collins, Catherine Hicks, Barry Watson, David Gallagher, Beverley Mitchell and Mackenzie Rosman.

As an executive producer, Biel, who shares two children with husband Justin Timberlake, said she's "looking for what I can watch with my kids on television."

"It's limited. I cannot watch a lot of these things with them, and they love TV, and it's my business. My husband and I are in this business together doing these things, and we can't share a lot of that with our kids," she explained.

The show, which initially focused on faith and its impacts on the community and family, will still honor that focus, according to Biel.

"I think the idea of whatever faith you want to have, that's important. That we don't have a lot on television, whether you believe that or go down that road or not," Biel shared. "There are a lot of people that really do want to walk down that road, so I think some kind of faith, some kind of family, community, and maybe something not so jaded, like something a little bit more glass-half-full. It's not that it's soft, because it's realistic."

Variety reported in May 2025 that none of the original cast members would be reprising their roles.

articles.title: What you didn’t see at the Daytime Emmys: Behind the scenes with Genie Francis, Tamara Tunie, Beth Maitland, and all the big winners
articles.summary: Gold Derby takes you inside the ceremony’s milestone wins, heartfelt tributes, and memorablebackstage moments.
articles.body:
Some fans may feel that holding the Daytime Emmys at the end of October is too late in the year, since the ceremony honors the best and brightest in soaps and other daytime programming from the previous calendar year.

But the good news for nominees, attendees, and press was the mild weather: Temperatures reached about 71 degrees at the ceremony, held at the Hollywood Palladium — a welcome change from the sweltering heat of earlier summer award ceremonies in Pasadena.

Best of all, all five soap operas — Beyond the Gates , The Bold and the Beautiful , Days of Our Lives , General Hospital , and The Young and the Restless — went home winners at the 2026 edition .

Hopes were high for Beyond the Gates , which entered the night with 15 nominations, a record for a soap opera in its first year of Emmy eligibility. (In 1988, The Bold and the Beautiful earned six nominations and won three, all in the Creative Arts categories.)

Beyond the Gates did not disappoint, taking home four awards Friday night . The show's biggest win went to Tamara Tunie, who won Best Lead Actress for her role as Anita Dupree. The actress submitted scenes related to Anita's breast cancer story.

"It's been incredible to have more than two Black actors on a show," Tunie told Gold Derby on the red carpet outside the Palladium before the show. "We're able to tell many stories and delve into different issues and situations."

The Young and the Restless ' Beth Maitland won her second Daytime Emmy on Friday night for Best Supporting Actress for her role as Traci Abbott. She had won the same award for the same role 41 years earlier, in 1985.

"It is a representation of the feeling of relevance," Maitland tells Gold Derby of her victory. "You can still be seen and heard."

The Bold and the Beautiful 's Scott Clifton, who took home Best Lead Actor for his role as Liam, told Gold Derby he had won four awards. In fact, he has won five times but owns only four statuettes.

"When I won my first Daytime Emmy [for Best Younger Actor in 2011 for playing Liam], they sent me home with it, but there was a rattling sound in the statuette," Clifton recalls. "I called NATAS and said, 'Hey, I think there's something wrong with my award. What should I do?' They said, 'This happens. No problem. We'll send you a new Emmy, and we'll also send you a box to return the old one to us.'"

Alas, the replacement award arrived, but the box never did. "I called," Clifton recalls. "Then I just gave up. The [first Emmy] is sitting in my attic, gathering dust."

Clifton's storyline aired in the first half of 2025, but actors submit reels from the eligibility period for consideration the following year, so the timing of a storyline within that period does not determine whether it can be submitted.

"That's a really astute point," Clifton tells Gold Derby. "If you have a brilliant performance in a film that comes out a week after the Oscars [you might not get noticed]. Daytime protects us."

The rules allow actors to submit up to 15 minutes of their work, but Clifton used about half that time. "I wanted to keep it under eight minutes," he says.

Clifton's reel included scenes establishing Liam's "fatal" brain tumor; scenes with his father, Bill (Don Diamont), in which Liam collapsed; and a third set of scenes in which Liam and Hope (Annika Noelle) admit that they both know he is dying.

Stories of death and dying also served other Emmy contenders well. The General Hospital writing team won for episodes involving the death of Monica (the late Leslie Charleson). The show also won its sixth consecutive Daytime Emmy for Best Daytime Drama Series for the somber storyline.

The Days of Our Lives directing team won for episodes involving the memorial for John Black (the late Drake Hogestyn).

"John represented a huge history, and he was very close to everyone, cast and crew, on-screen and off. What you saw was also a real-life celebration of [Drake's] life," said Noel Maxam, Days of Our Lives co-executive producer and director.

"Most people don't know that Drake and my wife [Abby] both died of pancreatic cancer, so the day and the episode took on a different meaning for me," Maxam says.

Days of Our Lives ' win in this category ended the General Hospital directors' six-year winning streak.

"I applaud General Hospital and all the directors there, and the directors at The Young and the Restless , too," Maxam says. "Our directors work very closely with each other. I'm so proud of our directors."

In addition to telling some of the most romantic stories on soaps, Days of Our Lives is also known for its memorable villains, including Stefano DiMera (the late Joe Mascolo) and Vivian Alamain (Louise Sorel). Maxam teases that another antagonist is joining the show's roster of baddies.

"There's so much coming up," Maxam says. "We have introduced, I think, one of the greatest supervillains to ever hit daytime."

General Hospital casting director Mark Teschner won his 12th Daytime Emmy for Best Casting in a Daytime Drama Series. His reel included performers new to Port Charles in 2025, including Erika Slezak (Ronnie, General Hospital ; ex-Viki, One Life to Live ), Rory Gibson (Michael), Carlo Rota (Jenz), and Chris McKenna (Jack). "We put 15 actors on our reel, and we started with Erika," Teschner tells Gold Derby. "I think we had a really good year. I love the cast. This cast is amazing."

A highlight of the night was the Lifetime Achievement Award, which went to legendary General Hospital actress Genie Francis. She won the Daytime Emmy for Best Supporting Actress in a Drama Series in 2007. Her husband, Jonathan Frakes ( Star Trek: The Next Generation ), presented the award.

While Laura Spencer is Francis' signature role, the video tribute package also acknowledged her other soap roles: Diana on Days of Our Lives , Ceara on All My Children , and Genevieve on The Young and the Restless . It also included Brett on the nighttime miniseries North and South .

Francis tells Gold Derby she was deeply touched by the number of co-stars, past and present, who paid tribute to her in the video package. Among those who sent shout-outs were Jonathan Jackson (ex-Lucky, General Hospital ), Mary Beth Evans (Kayla, Days of Our Lives ), and Parker Stevenson (Billy Hazard, North & South ).

Frakes referred to Francis' late leading man, General Hospital star Anthony Geary (Luke), who proclaimed in his acceptance speech after winning his first Daytime Emmy in 1982, "Genie Francis! Half of this is yours!"

"Wasn't it nice?" Francis said of the video tribute to her career. "I had no idea all those people were going to speak. It got to me."

Not much footage from Francis' early years on General Hospital appears to exist, but the package included early scenes of Francis and her TV mother, the late Denise Alexander (Lesley).

"Mostly, I just didn't want to disappoint her," Francis says of working with Alexander. "She was a big, big star, and I was there to be her daughter."

Persistence pays off for a Beyond the Gates star

Tunie's win came later in the awards show. Ambyr Michelle became the first acting winner from Beyond the Gates , winning Best Emerging Talent for her role as Eva Thomas.

"I don't just see an award. I see every audition, every rejection, every promise fulfilled," she said in her speech.

Gold Derby asked Michelle backstage about her speech and its universal appeal to anyone struggling to find professional fulfillment.

"Everybody may think that it's all butterflies and rainbows, but the journey to winning something like this is very hard," Michelle says. "I wanted my speech to be authentic and real. I feel like we broke out in our first year with 15 nominations. I want the show to go on for 100-plus years. I feel like this is just the start."

articles.title: I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
articles.summary: Meta said its Muse Charm should ship this year, but it’s also helping people code very similar gadgets with off-the-shelf hardware. We tried the Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C.
articles.body: Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta made AI look so stinking cute by giving it a squishy little face — and this holiday season, he wants to sell you a Muse Charm so you can carry your jolly AI helper around like a Tamagotchi. But I won’t be buying one, because we have Muse Charm at home. It cost just $50, and I’ve decided the learning experience was worth it. [Media: My version doesn’t sport cameras or a 5G cellular radio, but it really talks to Muse and has cute avatars, too! It doubles as a pocket watch and a remote camera viewfinder, and it can (theoretically) control my smart home. Or at least it can if you inject a lot of extra vibe code. Weeks ago, I paid $50 to get a 1.75-inch touchscreen computer pendant drop-shipped from China — specifically the Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C. Not only does the push-to-talk AI devkit look a lot like the Muse Charm, but it’s officially sanctioned by Meta. It’s one of the company’s first suggestions if you want to build a “Muse Gadget,” a device that uses Meta’s open-source code and tokens to directly connect to its Muse AI cloud. When the silver metal pocket watch arrived, it felt pretty useless to start. Setup was easy enough — I just plugged it into my PC and pointed Claude at Meta’s GitHub, then paired it to the Muse phone app. But even after I put Meta’s keys on the device, Muse originally thought I was sending it audio clips to transcribe rather than commands. After I cleared that up, Muse’s responses were still slow, and it didn’t answer me out loud. It was hard to tell what it was saying since it only showed a few words onscreen at a time, with no place to read full messages unless I whipped out my phone with its own Muse app. Meta’s build also only came with a single Jolly avatar that mostly just sat there and looked cute, and it wouldn’t automatically discover smart home gadgets like Amazon Echo or Google Home devices do. (This gadget really didn’t do anything useful after my initial install.) And though Meta AI software engineers Anant Narayanan and Jeremy Payne include a neat sample app showing how Muse Gadgets can stream video from your phone camera, the lack of a remote shutter button made it not so useful for taking photos. [Image: But a few sessions of Claude Code filled in almost all those holes. All I had to do was plug the Waveshare back into my PC, then ask Claude to reprogram each thing I wanted. When I complained to Claude that I couldn’t properly read or hear Muse’s replies to my asks, issues that others have mentioned as well, Claude built a conversation history page so I can swipe right to read what it said, and I plugged in a British AI voice from ElevenLabs that speaks its answers out loud. (The voice was the least soul-sucking of the ones in ElevenLabs’ free tier, my wife and I agree, even if it doesn’t match the Muse avatars’ cuddly vibe at all.) [Image: Thanks to Claude, I can now press a button to make my phone take a picture from across the room with a high-quality live preview, and my phone’s front-facing camera no longer displays upside down. Claude made fairly short work of adding a low-quality camera preview over Bluetooth, too, so I don’t need to be on home Wi-Fi to get photos from creative angles. [Image: [Image: I asked Claude to make a whole batch of different avatars like the ones Meta showed off during Meta Connect, and to add a Tamagotchi-like minigame where they need food, play, sleep, and a bath. When the game seemed too simple to capture any attention, I had it add four different levels of hunger, boredom, and dirt. I decided treats should make a crunchy mess and get avatars dirtier when they eat them, and that too much play should tire out a pet. My wish was Claude’s command. When I noticed I was accidentally letting go of the push-to-talk button too soon and making Muse choke on almost-empty audio, vibe coding fixed it minutes later by sending only audio over one second in length. The only obvious lag I’m seeing now is from Meta’s own servers — sometimes they’re responsive, sometimes they lag quite a bit. [Image: It was so easy to let Claude reprogram the pendant that I asked it to build a few features specifically for this video in this story, including a working pocket watch face with three hands that actually tells the time. (That took it 15 minutes; now, when I say the hardware looks like a pocket watch, you can see what I mean!) It even found, downloaded, trimmed, and loaded video clips of Zuck introducing the Muse Charm and installed a video player so I could play those clips on the Waveshare. I want you to understand I have no coding experience, and so I have no idea if any of this code is good. It might be fatally flawed. Nor do I trust Meta or its Muse agent with my email or my home network, particularly after hearing how it leaked one reviewer’s home address. (I put it on guest Wi-Fi from the get-go as a precaution.) That means I don’t really know how useful a Muse Charm may or may not be for those who do know how to code and are willing to take a bigger leap of faith. But after nearly dropping a bulky little silver pendant a couple of times, one with no more Muse functionality than my phone (and quite a bit less without additional code), I’m thinking Muse itself isn’t the reason to buy a dedicated compute pocket watch. The reason to have a dedicated piece of hardware is to do things you can’t do on the phone that’s already in your pocket, like coding the entire gadget to do whatever you want. Which makes me wonder: Will the actual Muse Charm be this freely programmable, or would the kind of people who’d buy one be better off with a development kit? I guess we’ll see when it ships.

articles.title: Keyboards of The Verge
articles.summary: From the strictly utilitarian to the ergonomic to the obsessive, these are the keyboards we use every day.
articles.body: What is a keyboard if not the original brain-computer interface? You can tap on a touchscreen or talk to the computer, but if your work involves getting information out of your head and into the computer, you’re probably spending a lot of time using a keyboard. We’ve written about many keyboards over the years, from the legendary Optimus Maximus to the ultra-luxe Seneca to even stranger fare. But I wanted to know what my coworkers actually use. As I’d hoped, there’s a wide range. Some of us are strictly utilitarian, optimizing for ergonomics or functionality. Others obsess over every detail of feel, sound, layout, and looks. Still others — maybe the most enlightened — just use whatever’s in front of them. NuPhy came up a lot. So did Keychron. The Apple Magic Keyboard has its stalwarts. The Kinesis Freestyle split is surprisingly well represented. And there are other, odder entries. These are the keyboards of The Verge. In this article Jay Peters, senior reporter [Image: Jay Peters’ Kinesis Freestyle Pro in a picture from 2021. Sadly, Gouda the cat passed away, but his spirit lives on through this photo. I currently use the Kinesis Freestyle Pro, and I’ve used it for so long that I’ve forgotten when I first got it. In the late 2010s, I had wrist pain that led me to try a lot of ergonomic keyboards so I could keep using computers. The Freestyle Pro — with its optional tenting add-ons that give the keyboard a significant angle and the palm rest accessories — just feels the best under my hands. If this keyboard broke, I’d buy another one the same day. Kallie Plagge, senior copy editor [Product: Logitech G713 wired mechanical keyboard and wristrest | For work, I use a simple Keychron K2. But for my gaming PC, I use the Logitech G713 wired mechanical keyboard — the one that comes with the cloud wrist rest. Did I mostly buy it for the wrist rest? Perhaps. But I do love the tenkeyless layout. My previous gaming keyboard had a number pad and two rows of programmable keys, which was cool, but I mostly used the number pad to type the alt code for em dashes. The G713, on the other hand, meets my gaming requirements without taking up half my desk. I’m not playing anything competitive on my PC that requires adjustable actuation points, so the GX red linear switches do the trick. (And they’re the right amount of clicky, unlike the overly loud ones on my K2.) So yeah, maybe I bought it for the sleek all-white look and the cute wrist rest, but it’s also a great keyboard, too. Danielle Steussy, product manager [Product: Apple Magic Keyboard with Touch ID and Numeric Keypad | I’m using Apple’s Magic Keyboard with the numeric keypad. Some version of Apple’s keyboard has been on my desk for over 20 years, starting with the Apple A1048 that came with my first Mac in college. I loved that keyboard (the sound of my fingertips hitting the keys — swoon!) and I wore it down to the point of keys falling off. Since then, I’ve stuck with Apple’s wireless keyboards. Honestly, it’s a pretty keyboard, but otherwise unremarkable, and blends in with my desk setup (which also is kind of the point, right?). My biggest complaints are that the key legends wear off faster than I’d like and the Bluetooth connection isn’t totally reliable. It’s not my favorite Apple product (by far), but after two decades of muscle memory, I’m not switching anytime soon. David Pierce, editor at large I really want to be a mechanical keyboard guy. I love typing on mechanical keyboards! I love the clackiness, the way they look on my desk, the huge personality upgrade that comes with them. But then I start typing notes during a call, and someone goes, “Sorry, what’s that noise in the background?” and I bail on my mechanical keyboard. I used Logitech’s MX Keys S for the last few years, and love that keyboard, but recently replaced it with an Apple Magic Keyboard (black keys, number pad) because I got tired of typing my 1Password password all the time. I bought a $200 keyboard for the Touch ID button. Ugh. Jacob Kastrenakes, executive editor [Image: Come on, you know where the letters are. My keyboard is probably the single dumbest thing I have ever spent money on, but it brings me joy every time I look at it. The setup matches a Boop Redux case with the GMK Dots keycaps and Silent Bluish White (V2) switches. I didn’t so much want to get deep into the mechanical keyboard hobby as I wanted to have this exact keyboard after I saw images of the Dots keycaps on the (original) Boop case floating around in around 2022. It looks cool, right? (Right?) From a practical standpoint, this is fully a downgrade from the Apple Magic Keyboard I was using before: It’s bigger and louder, with fewer keys, and I probably type a bit slower on it, too, owing to the longer key strokes. It’s also a few hundred dollars more expensive. But you know what? I think it looks really cool. Antonio G. Di Benedetto, laptop reviewer [Image: I’ve changed the keycaps and switches on this TM680 so many times. Since I review laptops and occasionally mechanical keyboards, I’m constantly changing what I type on. But one of my personal keyboards that remains close to my heart is my TM680 (aka the Gamakay LK67). It’s a cheap bare-bones 65-percent kit I bought from AliExpress in 2021. I was inspired by the video that YouTuber Scott “Keybored” Kim did on it, so I dabbled in modding it. I started with basic Gateron Milky Yellow linear switches and some crummy knockoff Evangelion keycaps, but I later upgraded to a much nicer MT3 3277 keycap set. I then spent hours individually lubricating and adding switch films to each of the Gaterons, lubing the stabilizers, inserting some foam into the base of the chassis, and adding layers of painter’s tape to the bottom of the PCB. This combination made my basic build sound and feel much better, and it shaped my preference for deeper, “thockier”-sounding boards that I still have today. My old TM680 is easily outdone by just about any budget board these days. Many switches now arrive pre-lubed from the factory, and even a sub-$100 keyboard can sound and feel nicer right out of the box. But doing the mods myself felt special. I doubt I’ll ever bother with all that work again, because lubing and filming switches is just too tedious and time-consuming, but I’m glad I at least experienced it once. And no matter how many new keyboards I test, I intend on keeping my TM680. TC Sottek, former senior editor [Product: Keychron K2 keyboard | I used to buy pretty expensive gaming keyboards that I can’t even name now without digging deep through email archives for receipts. I know I once spent nearly $200 on a full-size Razer mechanical keyboard with a numpad that took up a ton of desk space. The key travel felt amazing and it had a great sound. But what I really remember was knocking over a full glass of water on it. Oops! Farewell, keyboard. Unfortunately, this happened not once, not twice, but three times for me with relatively expensive keyboards over the years. Yes, I should have learned to contain liquids in bottles on my desk. But now I’ve settled for cheap–but–still-good options the same way I’ve done with the several pairs of earbuds I’ve ruined over the years. (Former serial AirPods Pro user here, now fully on board the Nothing Ear train.) I’m currently rocking a Keychron K2 with a 75-percent layout. It took me a minute to get my 120-plus WPM back on a cramped keyboard, but now it works just fine and I like the look. I’ll probably splurge again someday on a really compelling set of keycaps. Meredith Haggerty, senior reports editor [Image: This but with crumbs on it. I use the laptop that is attached to the M2 MacBook Air I was issued by my employer. It’s right there whenever I need it, but I think they should make a version that’s covered in way fewer crumbs. Emma Roth, news writer I have a toxic relationship with my keyboard, a Corsair K55 RGB Pro that I picked up for half the price at a thrift store a few years ago.
